name: Randomized Algorithms and Reservoir Sampling
intent: Understand why adding randomness can remove the bad inputs of an algorithm (quicksort with a random pivot), what expected cost versus worst-case cost means, and how reservoir sampling keeps a fair random sample from a stream whose length you do not know.
scenario: A service sorts a nightly export with a quicksort that takes the first element as pivot. When the export arrives already sorted, sorting 10,000 rows costs 49,995,000 comparisons instead of about 150,000. Picking the pivot at random fixes it: 154,586 comparisons on that same input, and over 20 different seeds on 1,000 sorted items the cost stays between 10,113 and 11,960. A second job needs 3 random log lines from a stream it can only read once. "Keep the first 3" is not random, "replace a random line half the time" is biased (counts from 1,679 to 4,928 where 3,000 is fair), and reservoir sampling is exactly fair (2,915 to 3,071) in 3 cells of memory.
problem: Many algorithms are fast on typical input and slow on a few awkward ones, and the awkward ones are often exactly the inputs real systems produce: sorted data, repeated keys, patterns an attacker can craft. A randomized algorithm uses random choices inside the algorithm so that no input is reliably bad; the cost becomes a random variable with a good expected value. Separately, some problems (a fair sample of a stream, a rough count, a membership test) have simple randomized solutions that look correct and are subtly wrong. The trap is treating "random" as one thing: it matters whether the result is always correct and only the time varies, whether the answer may be wrong with small probability, whether the choice is uniform, and whether the randomness must be predictable (tests) or unpredictable (security).

howItWorks.title: Why a fixed rule has bad inputs
howItWorks.text: Quicksort picks a pivot, splits the items into smaller and larger, and recurses on both parts. If the pivot is the first element and the input is sorted, nothing is ever smaller, so each split peels off one item: n minus 1, then n minus 2, and so on, n(n-1)/2 comparisons in total (499,500 for 1,000 items, 49,995,000 for 10,000). Any cheap fixed pivot rule (first, last, middle, median of three) has some input that does this. For the first or last element that input is simply sorted or nearly sorted data, which is common and not hostile; for middle or median of three it takes a contrived order, which an attacker can construct.

howItWorks.title: Let the algorithm roll the dice
howItWorks.text: Choose the pivot uniformly at random from the items in the current part. Now the input has no say: whatever order the items arrive in, the split is as good or as bad as the dice make it. A random pivot lands in the middle half of the items half the time, so the parts shrink geometrically and the expected number of comparisons is about 1.4 n log2 n at most. On 10,000 items that is 154,586 on sorted input, against 49,995,000 with the first element.

howItWorks.title: Expected versus worst case, and two kinds of randomness
howItWorks.text: The worst case did not disappear; it became a bad-luck event whose probability falls extremely fast as n grows. Over 20 seeds on 1,000 sorted items the count ranged from 10,113 to 11,960, a spread of about 18%, nowhere near 499,500. This is a Las Vegas algorithm: always correct, running time random. A Monte Carlo algorithm is the other kind: always fast, but the answer may be wrong with a small, controlled probability (Bloom filters and probabilistic primality tests are of this kind). Say which one you are using. Randomness is not free either: on shuffled input the first-element pivot took 146,101 comparisons and the random pivot 160,879.

howItWorks.title: Reservoir sampling: a fair sample of a stream you read once
howItWorks.text: To keep k items from a stream of unknown length, store the first k. For each later item number i (counting from 1), pick a random integer from 1 to i; if it is at most k, the new item replaces the stored item in that slot, otherwise it is discarded. After the whole stream of n items, every item is in the sample with probability exactly k/n: item i enters with probability k/i, and each later item then evicts it with just the chance that keeps the total at k/n. Memory is k cells, however long the stream. One pass over 1,000,000 items with k = 5 wrote to the reservoir only 64 times.

howItWorks.title: Seeds: reproducible for tests, unpredictable for security
howItWorks.text: A pseudo-random generator started from a seed produces the same sequence every time. For tests and simulations, that is what you want: log the seed, and a failure can be replayed. For anything an adversary profits from predicting (the pivot of a sort that serves requests, hash seeds), seed from the operating system's secure source, because a guessable seed brings back the bad inputs; for secrets such as tokens, draw every value from a cryptographically secure generator, since an ordinary generator can often be predicted from its outputs even when its seed is secret. Libraries differ, so check what your language's default generator promises.

pros: No fixed input is reliably bad: sorted, reversed and crafted inputs all cost about the same as random ones
Simple to implement: a random pivot is one extra line, reservoir sampling is five
Reservoir sampling uses k cells and one pass, whatever the stream length, and is exactly uniform
Often the simplest or only practical solution for huge or unbounded data
cons: The guarantee is about expectation: a single run can be unlucky, which matters for hard deadlines
Runs are not reproducible unless you control and log the seed, which complicates debugging
Some cost on easy input: the random pivot needed 160,879 comparisons where the first element needed 146,101
Randomness is easy to get subtly wrong: modulo bias, weak generators, shared generators across threads
whenToUse: A fixed rule has known bad inputs that real data can produce (sorted data and a first-element pivot)
You need a uniform random sample from a stream, a log or a table too large to hold
Approximate answers are acceptable and a small, quantified chance of error buys a big saving
Randomized tests and simulations, with the seed recorded
whenNotToUse: Hard real-time work where the occasional unlucky run is unacceptable: use an algorithm with a deterministic worst case, such as a heap-based or merge-based sort
When you must reproduce a result exactly and cannot store the seed
When a library already does it: use the built-in sort (many combine quicksort with a fallback, or use a merge-based sort) rather than writing your own
When all the data fits in memory and you need a shuffle: shuffling and taking k items is simpler than reservoir sampling
pitfalls: "Replace a random slot with probability 1/2" looks fair and is not: later items need only win one coin flip, earlier ones must survive them all. Over 10,000 runs the counts ranged from 1,679 to 4,928 where 3,000 is fair. The replace chance must be k/i, which falls as the stream grows
Keeping the first k, or every n-th item, as a "sample": it is only random if the stream has no order or period, and logs, files and tables nearly always do

Taking a random number modulo n without thinking: when the generator's range is not a multiple of n, some values are slightly more likely. Negligible for a toy, real for large ranges or fairness-critical draws; use the language's bounded-integer function
Using a predictable seed (a timestamp, 1) in production for something an attacker benefits from guessing, such as the pivot choice or a hash seed. Predictable randomness brings the bad input back
Not logging the seed of a randomized test: a failure that cannot be replayed is nearly useless
Sharing one non-thread-safe generator between threads, or seeding every worker identically so they all draw the same numbers
Calling a Monte Carlo result exact: say what the error probability is, or choose a Las Vegas algorithm if you need certainty
Reading "expected O(n log n)" as a promise per request: a service with a strict latency target cares about the tail, not the mean

roles.label: Data stream
roles.description: Items arrive one at a time, in some order and of a length you may not know.

roles.label: Seeded generator
roles.description: Produces the dice rolls: the same seed gives the same sequence.

roles.label: Quicksort
roles.description: Picks a pivot, splits the items around it and recurses on both sides.

roles.label: Reservoir
roles.description: k cells holding the current sample; each new item may replace one.

quiz.question: A quicksort that takes the first element as pivot is fed 10,000 items that are already sorted. What happens, and what does a random pivot change?
options: It stays fast, because sorted input needs no swaps and a random pivot only adds cost to it.
It does about 150,000 comparisons either way, since quicksort is always O(n log n) on any input.
About 50 million: each split peels off one item. A random pivot ignores input order.
It fails, because sorted input cannot be partitioned at all; a random pivot only makes it work.
quiz.explanation: With the first element as pivot, a sorted input splits into 0 and n-1 items every time: 49,995,000 comparisons for n = 10,000. A random pivot makes the split independent of the order, so the expected cost is about n log n (154,586 here); O(n log n) is an expectation for random pivots, not for every fixed rule.

quiz.question: You must keep 3 random items from a stream of unknown length that can only be read once. Which approach gives every item the same chance of being kept?
options: Keep the first 3 items, since they were drawn without bias from the start of the stream.
Keep 3 cells; item number i replaces a random cell with chance 3/i, else it is dropped.
After the first 3 items, replace a random cell with probability 1/2 for every later item.
Keep every n-th item, where n is the number of items you expect to see in the stream.
quiz.explanation: The replace probability k/i falls as the stream grows, which exactly balances the longer time early items have to be evicted, so every item ends with chance k/n. Fixed probabilities (1/2) favour late items, and first-k or every-n-th are not random at all.

quiz.question: Why would a production service pick its quicksort pivot with a generator seeded from the operating system rather than seeding it with the number 1?
options: A seed of 1 makes the sort slower, since it would pick the pivots in increasing order.
The operating system's generator never repeats a number, which any seeded one will do.
A fixed seed makes the sort return wrong answers on some inputs, however large they are.
Anyone who knows the seed can craft input where every pivot is bad again.
quiz.explanation: The sort is still correct with any seed, and the expected cost holds only while the choices are unpredictable to whoever supplies the input. A known seed lets an attacker compute the pivots and build input for which they are all poor. For tests the opposite holds: use a fixed seed, and log it.
